newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Germans wary of buying fuel because of strong dollar.
newsitem.headline: Germans wary of buying fuel because of strong dollar.

text.p: German gas oil users, deterred from buying in the past year because of the high dollar-based prices of the product, now have two additional factors to contend with -- the dollar's steep rise against the mark and the sale of Germany's crude reserves.
The result, say German gas oil traders, is that the average consumer in Germany, Europe's largest heating oil market, is even more reluctant to buy than before.

On Monday, the dollar rose to its highest level against the mark since August 1991, just short of DM1.80. The rise coincided with a strengthening of dollar-denominated IPE gas oil futures. Trading of imported heating oil barges collapsed with almost no wholesaler demand, dealers said.

"Normally, the (IPE) rise would have provoked a sudden pick up of demand, but yesterday there was nothing. The IPE did of course come off later, but the dollar seems to have kept people away," one German trader said.

The dollar's sharp rise did at least spur a flurry of buying from German inland refiners as price rises for domestically produced heating oil lagged those for imported material. Traders said the buying had since tailed off.
"People don't believe the dollar can keep on rising, although of course they've thought that before and it has" said one German trader.
On Tuesday, the dollar held above the DM1.79 level after a brief dip below. The dollar has risen since Friday morning to its six year high.
The decision by Germany to sell crude from its oil reserves starting early August has also cooled consumers' interest.

Dealers said consumers would probably have ignored the news, but that a major German tabloid newspaper had advised its sizeable readership to delay their purchases, with a front page article saying prices would fall when the German crude is sold.
"The whole domestic market has been complaining...as they have an enormous impact on the decision (to buy)," one German gas oil trader said.
"It may not be right, but people are reading this and that's what they believe," said another.
